title: Your policy may not cover the thing you fear.
subtitle: Most policies have windows and exclusions. Both are readable, and almost nobody reads them.

text: Cover for a pre-existing condition often depends on when you bought.
sub: Many insurers tie it to a period after your deposit date, and the length varies by insurer and by country. Read the certificate, and ask before you buy rather than after.

items.head: Medical evacuation at sea
items.body: Removing someone from a ship mid-ocean is the most expensive thing that can happen to a voyage.

items.head: Pre-existing conditions
items.body: Cover often hinges on a purchase window after deposit. Confirm the exact terms with the insurer in writing.

items.head: Cancel for any reason
items.body: Where it exists it is usually an add-on with its own deadline and a partial payout.

items.head: Missed departure
items.body: Check whether a delayed flight to embarkation is covered, and under what conditions.

points.label: Medical
points.value: Illness ashore or onboard, and the cost of the care that follows you home.

points.label: Evacuation
points.value: Distance from a hospital, rather than severity, is what drives the bill.

points.label: Cancellation
points.value: A parent's illness at home ends more voyages than anything at sea.

points.label: Delay
points.value: Flights, not ships, cause most of the disruption people claim for.

text: Buy the policy when you pay the deposit, not when you pack.
sub: The clauses that matter most are usually tied to a date you have already passed by the time you start reading them.

text: Read three things: the medical limit, the evacuation limit, the exclusions.
sub: If the evacuation figure looks generous, check whether it is combined with the medical limit or genuinely separate from it.

title: Send this to the person you'd travel with
body: I don't sell the policy, so the questions are the whole of my interest — ask, and I'll tell you what I'd put to an insurer before signing.
